transcript:
[00:00] Jordan: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick roll call, and then we will jump into the benchmark slides.
[00:08] Alex: Yep I'm here, Dana and Omar with me.
[00:12] Dana: here.
[00:15] Priya: Priya here from Redwood. I'll own the perf details today.
[00:20] Jordan: Cool. So quick agenda: go over the week-over-week numbers, compare to the baseline provider runs you shared, talk tuning we tried this week, then outline next steps.
[00:34] Alex: Sounds good, interested mostly in p95 latency and how that scales at 100 and 500 concurrent requests.
[00:40] Priya: Right, and we ran a 3-hour bench with the synthetic chat workload you provided and also re-played the baseline provider logs you uploaded. Two things to call out up front: our hosted config showed ~18% better p95 on 1k token conv flows, but at high concurrency throughput leveled because of batching/backpressure.
[01:05] Dana: When you say "1k token conv flows" do you mean 1,000 tokens per response or 1,000 token context? Our test is mixed, some are long context.
[01:12] Priya: Good call — sorry, I mean 1k total sequence length context (prompt + response). For long context the KV cache hit rate matters a lot. We saw ~72% KV hit for repeated prefixes in your dataset.
[01:28] Omar: We should call out our baseline provider was using model-variant B quantized 4-bit, and they had a custom batching layer. They also had a different sequence truncation strategy.
[01:38] Jordan: Right, that's key. The baseline provider's batching was tuned for throughput with larger micro-batches. Redwood by default favors latency SLOs which results in smaller batch windows unless you opt into throughput mode.
[01:50] Alex: Do you have numbers that show the tradeoff? Like p95 vs tokens/sec at 500 concurrency?
[01:56] Priya: Yes. Slide 3 — in our hosted run at 500 concurrent sessions, tokens/sec peaked at about 22k T/s with p95 ~420ms for 256-token average responses. Baseline provider peaked at 28k T/s but p95 was ~620ms. For the 1k-token flows, our p95 moved to ~1.2s while they were around 1.4s. So we win latency but lose some aggregate throughput.
[02:24] Dana: Hmm, that matches what we saw. But our cost model also matters — the baseline provider's effective token cost was lower because of denser batching on cheaper GPU types.
[02:35] Priya: Right — and we flagged a couple of levers: 1) increase batch window to shift towards throughput, 2) enable more aggressive quantization for the model variant (we tested int4 and saw ~10-12% latency improvement but some accuracy delta), 3) tune compilation/kernel selection for long sequence.
[02:54] Jordan: We also tried prefix caching and observed significantly lower p50/p90 for repeated user prompts. But for cold-starts the baseline's dense batching helped their aggregate T/s.
[03:06] Alex: Any surprises in memory or OOM events during your run? Our on-prem env had some memory pressure when we tried the baseline's settings.
[03:15] Priya: No OOMs in our hosted runs. On the on-prem mirror we did see higher memory footprint when we used the same aggressive batching plus the baseline's longer context checkpoints. That suggests their infra uses slightly different kernel selection/tiling. We need to profile GPU kernel allocation to be sure.
[03:31] Omar: We can share the mem profiles from the baseline provider. I uploaded a sample earlier but can send the full set.
[03:36] Jordan: Please do — that's helpful.
[03:40] Priya: Quick note on KV — we had a mis-transcription in the first report calling it "K-V cash" so ignore that, it's cache. The effective hit-rate was the main driver for p95 on conversational re-runs.
[03:51] Dana: Regarding security/compliance: the baseline provider claims SOC2 and has audit export; Redwood you mentioned audit logs and KMS support earlier, any differences?
[04:00] Jordan: Redwood supports SOC2, SSO/SAML, RBAC, and we integrate with customer KMS/HSM for Private deployments. For the hosted POC we have encryption-at-rest and detailed audit logs; we can export the same format your compliance team expects.
[04:15] Alex: Good. Also, how does the private/on-prem runtime affect latency/throughput? We assume network hops for VPC peering and routing might add tail latency.
[04:25] Priya: Yes, VPC adds networking tail but the advantage is lower cross-tenant interference and you can choose a dedicated GPU profile which improves throughput consistency. In our emulated on-prem run we saw similar median latency but higher p95 variance due to network jitter in the test harness.
[04:44] Jordan: On that note, one of the upcoming runs should be the on-prem deep dive where our infra engineer will walk through kernel selection and compilation flags. That's what we suggested for Oct 8.
[04:55] Dana: Fine with that. Can you call out the specific tests you want from us for that run?
[05:00] Priya: We need: full baseline logs, the 95th-tail synthetic workload (not averaged), and exact model variant/config the baseline used. Also details on GPU type and driver versions.
[05:13] Omar: We'll get that.
[05:15] Jordan: Back to tuning — Priya you said quantization improved latency but impacted quality. Did you get any automated eval diffs?
[05:24] Priya: We ran the eval harness on a 500-sample prompt set. int4 introduced a ~2.1% drop in our metric (ROUGE/EM-ish surrogate) on the narrow generation tasks; for conversational safety/intent tasks the delta was <1%. We can push a larger eval if you want.
[05:41] Dana: We care about final user experience, so if int4 hurts high-precision outputs we may not accept it across the board. Could be okay for chat summarization.
[05:51] Priya: Exactly, most customers use hybrid profiles — quantize some layers or use int8 for mid-tier throughput. Redwood Optimize can recommend per-workload quantization.
[06:03] Alex: Any notes about model fallback strategies? Baseline provider had an automatic fallback to smaller model when overloaded.
[06:10] Jordan: Redwood supports rollouts and automatic fallback policies — you can set route priority: primary low-latency model, fallback to cheaper variant on capacity pressure. The platform's smart routing will do that and keep traceability.
[06:22] Priya: Also we instrument token-level traces so you can see where latency spikes. That was useful in the run where an outlier RPC to a metadata service caused p99 spikes.
[06:33] Omar: We saw one p99 spike ~4.2s in your run, do you have the trace?
[06:36] Priya: yes, linked in the spreadsheet; it traced to a cache miss plus a GC cycle on the shard, plus a network retry for a storage call. We can correlate to environment markers.
[06:47] Dana: Are there configuration changes we can make without changing models? Like adjusting the autoscaler thresholds?
[06:53] Jordan: Yep, autoscaler target latency and queue depth are knobs. You can lower target latency which will reserve more GPUs earlier, costing more but flattening tail latency. We recommended for your workload a 20% lower latency target for peak windows.
[07:06] Alex: Cost tradeoffs — can you show cost per 1M tokens at our observed T/s for both Redwood and baseline?
[07:13] Priya: We have an estimate in the sheet. For the hosted config we estimate $X per 1M tokens (redacted in transcript), baseline was ~15% cheaper at peak throughput due to cheap GPU choices and denser batching. But when you factor in p95 and error-retries, effective user-facing cost narrows.
[07:35] Jordan: We'll put the full cost model in the spreadsheet; that's one of the next deliverables.
[07:40] Alex: Great. On the test side, I want to make sure our synthetic workload covers edge-case long-context flows and cold-start spikes at mornings.
[07:50] Priya: We'll add that to the test matrix. Also we'll run a separate cold-start bench for 2-hour morning spike profile.
[07:58] Omar: Regarding private deployment, what's the effort to onboard — how long to get a Private control plane vs Dedicated reserved capacity?
[08:05] Jordan: Dedicated capacity is quickest — reserve slots and we map GPU pools, typically 1–3 weeks for initial capacity depending on region. Private (VPC/on-prem) is more involved: about 4–8 weeks depending on network approvals and KMS/HSM integration. On-prem (air-gapped) is longer and requires ops collaboration.
[08:24] Dana: That's in line with our timeline. We aim to decide by late October.
[08:29] Jordan: Good. Any other questions from the bench results?
[08:33] Alex: One more: Did you compare decoding strategies? baseline provider used slightly larger beam/temperature defaults.
[08:40] Priya: Yes, we normalized decoding across runs to greedy with same top-k where applicable. The baseline's reported higher throughput partly came from lower sampling variance in their model tuning, but we kept generation config consistent for apples-to-apples.
[08:56] Dana: Ok, next steps recap?
[08:59] Jordan: Jordan to share raw spreadsheet & logs; Priya to run per-shard latency profiling and new quantization evals; Dana/Omar to provide full baseline logs and VPC details; schedule on-prem deep dive for Oct 8.
[09:12] Alex: Sounds good. Thanks everyone.
[09:15] Priya: Thanks, we'll follow up in email with calendar invite and links.
[09:20] Jordan: End.
